job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Lena Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied business management with an accounting minor at Eastbrook University and graduated in July. I live with my parents and my grandparents above our family bakery, Costa's Bakehouse, on Mill Road. I'm up at five to help with the morning bake, then I use AI tools to run the bakery's books and ordering until noon, and in the afternoon I apply for jobs and chase a few freelance bookkeeping leads. On Sundays the whole family goes to church together.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of all that, and what part do you still like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hardest thing is that I'm busy all day and still not earning a salary of my own. I've applied for about fifty jobs and had five interviews. What I love is making a messy small business tidy: at my internship at a local property agent, Pike and Sons, I set up their invoicing and cut their late payments by a third.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Plenty of people talked it up and the real world doesn't change that quickly. But I'd say the tools I use already save me hours, so I'd keep using them, hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in the same position I'm in now. I have some debt, about a month and a half of savings and no salary, though the bakery gives me a bed and a bit of pocket money. The routine bits, like invoices and ordering, are what AI does for me, so I'm slightly ahead of the game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the bakery's books on AI and use that as a case study to sell bookkeeping to other small family firms on Mill Road. I'd aim for five clients by spring, at a fair monthly fee. I'd keep applying for salaried jobs too, one or two a week, for the security and the experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, hopeful even. I'm not rushing, and I know I've got something to build on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day for the bakery. How does that fit with the idea that it's mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery has survived because it does a few things well and everyone knows it. My granddad says, 'Know your customer and your costs.' That's the same lesson as a ledger: know where your money goes and who owes you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the bakery teach you about how businesses actually survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My gran was the first to say it, actually: 'A bakery that's lazy with its books closes.' Fixing the books made us 400 a month better off, which is the best argument for what I do.

I'd tell friends to keep using what **saves time**.
think: I'm in the **same position** as now, but the routine tasks AI does are ones I already use.
I have **some debt** and about a month and a half of savings.
do: Use the bakery's books as a **case study** to sell bookkeeping to family firms.
Aim for **five clients by spring** at a fair monthly fee.
Keep applying for **salaried jobs**, one or two a week, for security.
feel: It feels **fine and hopeful**, because I have something to build on.
S0.quote: A bakery that's lazy with its books closes.
fieldNote: Lena's **family business** gives her a bed, a case study and a reason to feel uneasy, not anxious.
She **keeps a salaried job** search going alongside the freelance plan.
Her **tools-first habit** puts her slightly ahead of her peers.

Keep running the bakery's books on AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but a fair one. Firms that adapt will do well, and the rest will complain. I'd say people should work and learn instead of waiting for government to rescue them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a lot of bookkeeping and basic accounting gets done by software, so plain bookkeeping isn't a business for long. The value moves to advice: telling a baker whether to buy a second oven. I want to be that person, but I know some competitors will have the same idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the bookkeeping idea into an advice service, with software doing the entry and me doing the thinking, for local family businesses. I'd get a first salaried job at a firm that's adopting AI, to learn how they do it. I'd also put 200 a month into a savings account for a rainy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and slightly nervy. I like being early, but I know early can also mean wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you think small-business bookkeeping heads in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plain bookkeeping goes to software, tax returns for simple businesses too. What stays is the question, 'What should I do with this?', and the human who knows the family and the street. That's where the money will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the bakery's own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to put the ordering and till reports on AI this year, and keep the bakers, because the loaf is what people come for. We'd save about ten hours a week for my mum, which she'd spend on customers.

say: I'd say it's a **big change but a** fair one, and firms that adapt will do well.
I'd say people should **work and learn** instead of waiting for rescue.
think: Plain bookkeeping goes to software, so the **value moves to advice**, like whether to buy a second oven.
Some competitors will have **the same idea**.

Take a **salaried job** at a firm already adopting AI to learn how.

S1.quote: Plain bookkeeping goes to software, tax returns for simple businesses too.
fieldNote: Lena **sees her own planned** business shrinking and moves up to advice, an adaptive move.

steps.text: Offer advice-led accounts support to family businesses
Take a job at a firm that is adopting AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is not a time for blame but for building. I'd say families and small firms should hold together, and that anyone who makes money from AI should pay into a fund for those who lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared but I'd move. If AI does all thinking work by 2028, my degree and my bookkeeping idea are both at risk, but the bakery is physical and local. Robots take three more years to do what my family does with its hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the bakery at the centre. I'd learn to bake properly from my dad and gran, use AI to cut the paperwork and ordering to almost nothing, and start a second line, like online pre-orders, to grow sales. I'd keep applying for work, but I'd stop spending on anything but the family and church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a drumroll before something big. I'm shaky, but I think I'd be more alive than sorry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandparents, and when?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grandparents on the first Sunday after lunch, because they like bad news with a bit of bread. They've seen worse. My granddad survived a flood in 1987 and says every bad year ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of the bakery would you protect, and which would you change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd protect the hands: the bake, the shop counter, the customers. I'd change everything behind: ordering, books, social posts. That way the family does the part that's hard to copy.

say: I'd say this isn't a time for blame but for **building**, and AI profits should fund a safety net.
I'd say **families and small firms** should hold together.
think: My degree and bookkeeping idea are both at risk, but the **bakery is physical** and local.

S2.quote: I'd protect the hands: the bake, the shop counter, the customers. I'd change everything behind: ordering, books, social posts.
fieldNote: Lena is anxious but **not alarmed** because the family bakery is hands-on and she'd move quickly.
She **protects the physical part** of the business and automates the desk part.
Her family's **resilience stories** shape how she tells bad news.

steps.text: Learn the full bake from my dad and gran

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway, and the best thing we can do is get started. I'd tell my friends to build something real, and I'd tell the government to reward work and training, not just hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel okay, actually. In five years I could get a first job, learn what AI-driven firms do, build my own client base and have savings. I'd still be a little nervous that it moves faster than I plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a salaried job for two years, learn the tools at scale and save half of my pay. Then I'd launch my advice firm for local businesses in 2029, with the bakery as my reference client. I'd keep investing a bit each month in a simple fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a to-do list with a deadline, which suits me. I get a bit giddy and have to remind myself to rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is your plan different with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. I'd help the bakery behind the scenes and keep my own firm, because the two feed each other. The bakery gives me credibility and customers, and my firm gives the bakery better numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in the family business or go out on your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The main change is that I'd work for someone else first. With two years I'd skip that and go straight to the family business. With five years I can afford to learn on someone else's money.

I'd say government should **reward work and training**, not just hand out money.

fieldNote: More time lets Lena **work for someone else** first, a clear difference from her two-year plan.

steps.text: Take a salaried job for two years and save half

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it. I'd say we should rebuild trades and local business, and I'd say it to anyone who'll listen, with a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm really quite calm. Ten years is plenty to qualify, build a firm, save a deposit and probably marry. I'd also say the bakery will still be here, and that's a comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in a firm for two years, then start my own, and I'd get a professional accounting qualification on the side. I'd invest monthly, learn new tools as they appear, and maybe open a second bakery or a bakery-supply line with my brother. I'd also say a prayer every Sunday and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting, like standing at the foot of a mountain I want to climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, how big do you think you could build things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have a small firm with three or four staff and a share in the bakery, married with a child. And I'd want to hire local young people, since I know how hard the start is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong, even with all that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What could go wrong is that I get complacent or overreach, like expanding too fast. Or something happens in the family, like health. I'd keep a cash buffer, for those reasons.

I'd say we should **rebuild trades** and local business.

The **bakery will still be** here, which is a comfort.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, though I'd cope better than most. The risk is not enough time to build what I'm planning. What would help is small-business grants for young people, and training and apprenticeship places that are open to anyone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that adaptive doesn't mean I don't have doubts. I use the tools every day, I pray about it, and I still lie awake sometimes. I want to be useful to my family and my town, and I hope that's still worth something.

headlineQuote: I use the tools every day, I pray about it, and I still lie awake sometimes.
portrait: Lena is a 23-year-old **business management graduate** living above her family's bakery on Mill Road, with fifty applications and five interviews.
She uses AI daily for the bakery's books, has some debt and a **bookkeeping side plan**.
She is traditional, church-going and pro-market, and wants **apprenticeships** and small-business support, not handouts.
Her moods run from uneasy to anxious and then **calm at ten years**, on a family base.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, since there'd be too little time to build what she is planning.
whatWouldHelp: **Small-business grants** for young people and open training and apprenticeship places would help.
